title: What to burn in a stove or fireplace, and what never to
summary: Dry, clean wood is the fuel. Treated, painted and glued wood, plastics, salt-water driftwood, railway ties and garbage put poisons in the smoke and ash or corrode the stove and chimney; armfuls of paper or cardboard and dry Christmas trees can start chimney fires. How to spot treated wood and read a pallet's stamp.

steps.text: Burn dry, split, unpainted wood: under 20% moisture (EPA best burn, Drolet Part 1).

Treat any wood that is green or brown-tinted, smells of tar or oil, or came from a deck, fence, dock, pole, tie or playground as treated, and don't burn it. Plain-looking wood isn't cleared by its look: aged CCA looks like untreated wood and residential treated wood has little smell (Health Canada treated wood, Health Canada 2011).
steps.warn: CCA-treated wood sends arsenic up with the smoke and leaves it in the ash (USFS arsenic, Health Canada 2011).

steps.text: Read a pallet's stamp before you break it up: HT or DH is heat-treated; MB or SF means fumigated, so leave it (CFIA D-98-08). Skip painted pallets and any with spills.
Light with a few sheets of newspaper and kindling, never armfuls of paper or cardboard (NRCan wood heating, CSIA white paper).
steps.warn: Never gasoline, kerosene or waste oil to start or feed a fire (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1).

steps.text: No plastics, foam, vinyl, painted wood, particleboard, MDF, salt-water driftwood, garbage or evergreen boughs (EPA best burn, Drolet Part 1, CPSC 611).

Coal only in a stove whose label lists it (EPA catalytic, Drolet Part 1). Plywood and OSB: don't; every maker and agency says no (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1). The notes give our own emergency-only judgement, which is not a rule.

Let ash from anything doubtful go fully cold in a lidded metal can outside (it can hold live embers for days: Drolet Part 1), then bag it and keep it out of gardens (Health Canada 2011, EPA trash burning).

notes:
## The table
| Material | Burn it? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Firewood, split and dry (under 20% moisture) | Yes | The fuel stoves are made for (EPA best burn, Drolet Part 1). See [Firewood](#guides/skill_firewood) |
| Clean scrap lumber and offcuts you know are untreated, dry and not painted or coated | Yes | Woodheat accepts it (Woodheat poison). Lumber pulled out of a building is not that: Drolet and the US rule ban construction or demolition debris, and old wood may carry lead paint or treatment (Drolet Part 1, 40 CFR 60.532, Health Canada lead paint) |
| Pallets stamped HT or DH, plain wood, unpainted, no spills | Only if your stove's manual allows it; see the stamp section | Woodheat says packing skids can be burned if not painted or coated (Woodheat poison), but the US rule bans pallets in certified stoves (40 CFR 60.532), though Drolet's list doesn't name them |
| Pallets stamped MB or SF | No | Fumigated with a chemical (CFIA D-98-08) |
| Newspaper and kindling to light the fire | Yes, a few sheets | Starting a fire with paper and cardboard starters is allowed (Drolet Part 1, 40 CFR 60.532) |
| Wet, green, rotten or mouldy wood | No | Smoky fire, creosote (EPA best burn, Drolet Part 1) |
| Pressure-treated wood: green (CCA) or brown (ACQ, copper azole) | Never | Chemicals in the smoke and ash; CCA holds arsenic (Health Canada treated wood, USFS arsenic) |
| Railway ties, utility poles, old posts and pilings | Never | Creosote, pentachlorophenol or CCA (Health Canada treated wood) |
| Painted, stained, varnished or coated wood | Never | EPA says no painted or coated wood (EPA best burn); old paint may hold lead (Health Canada says homes built before 1960 probably have it) and heating lead paint makes toxic fumes with lead (Health Canada lead paint) |
| Plywood, OSB and other glued wood | No | NRCan says plywood and particleboard release a toxic cloud of chemicals, and EPA, CMHC and Drolet say not to burn them (NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat, EPA best burn, Drolet Part 1). The emergency-only exception below is our own judgement, not a rule |
| Particleboard, MDF and laminate-faced boards | No | EPA and Drolet name particleboard, and EPA bans any wood with glue on or in it; EPA says pressed-wood products give off formaldehyde when burned (EPA best burn, Drolet Part 1, EPA trash burning) |
| Vinyl siding, PVC pipe, other plastics, foam | Never | PVC makes hydrochloric acid; chlorine makes dioxins (EPA trash burning, EPA best burn) |
| Asphalt shingles, tar paper, construction and demolition debris | Never | Asphalt products, building debris and anything with asbestos in it are all banned fuels (Drolet Part 1, 40 CFR 60.532) |
| Salt-water driftwood | Never | Dioxins; corrodes stainless steel (Woodheat poison, DuraVent DTC) |
| Glossy magazines, coloured or wrapping paper | No | Coloured inks; flash fires (EPA best burn, CPSC 611) |
| Cardboard and paper by the armful | No | Flash fires; often burned right before a chimney fire (CPSC 611, CSIA white paper) |
| Garbage | Never | Dioxins in the smoke and the ash (Woodheat poison, Drolet Part 1) |
| Christmas trees and evergreen boughs | No | Explode and flare; add creosote (Iowa State trees, CPSC 611) |
| Coal | Only if the stove's label lists it | Drolet's stoves say no; it can poison a catalyst (Drolet Part 1, EPA catalytic) |
| Waste oil, gasoline, kerosene, paint, thinner | Never | Banned fuels; liquid fuels give more fire than you bargained for (Drolet Part 1, NRCan wood heating) |
| Yard waste, leaves, manure, animal remains | No | Banned fuels (Drolet Part 1, 40 CFR 60.532) |
| Wax-and-sawdust fire logs | Fireplaces; stoves only if the maker allows | Many are made for open fireplaces only (EPA best burn); Drolet bans logs of wax-impregnated sawdust or with additives in its stoves and allows plain compressed-sawdust logs with caution (Drolet Part 1) |

Drolet's list of banned fuels matches the US rule for new stoves closely (Drolet Part 1, 40 CFR 60.532). The differences: Drolet adds coal, and the US rule adds pallets and anything the stove's manual and certification tests don't include. Drolet warns that burning the listed fuels can make more carbon monoxide than hardwood (Drolet Part 1).

## Treated wood: how to tell, and why not
- **What it looks like:** today's residential treated lumber (ACQ or copper azole) comes in shades of brown; CCA is light green when new but can look like plain wood once it has aged; most has little or no smell. Railway ties are treated with creosote, which smells of petroleum, and utility poles with pentachlorophenol or CCA (Health Canada treated wood).
- **Where it is:** decks, fences, docks and pilings, utility poles, playgrounds and outdoor construction lumber (Health Canada 2011, Health Canada treated wood). CCA is no longer sold for home building in Canada (Health Canada treated wood) and stopped being made for home use in the US at the end of 2003 (EPA CCA), so older decks and fences may still be CCA.
- **Why not:** burning releases the preservatives into the smoke, and the ash can hold dangerous concentrations of the same chemicals (Health Canada 2011). In lab tests 22 to 77% of the arsenic in CCA wood went up with the smoke, mostly as particles, along with smaller shares of the copper and chromium (USFS arsenic). Health Canada says never burn treated wood, indoors or out (Health Canada treated wood).
- **If you can't tell:** treated wood can't always be recognised; if you're unsure, don't burn it (Health Canada 2011).

## Reading a pallet stamp
Pallets that cross borders carry the ISPM 15 mark: the IPPC symbol on the left, then a two-letter country code and the producer's number (for example CA-123), then the treatment code (CFIA D-98-08, ISPM 15).

| Code | Means | Burn it? |
|---|---|---|
| HT | Heat treatment | Yes, if plain and clean |
| DH | Dielectric heating | Yes, if plain and clean |
| MB | Fumigated with methyl bromide | No |
| SF | Fumigated with sulphuryl fluoride | No |

Codes from CFIA D-98-08 and ISPM 15. The mark must be legible and permanent and is never hand drawn (CFIA D-98-08, ISPM 15); older pallets may carry an earlier version of it (ISPM 15). Methyl bromide is an ozone-depleting gas whose use is being cut back (ISPM 15). We found no source that measured what an MB pallet gives off when burned; it is chemically treated, so leave it when plain wood or HT pallets are around. No stamp tells you nothing about treatment. Painted or coloured pallets and any pallet that carried or soaked up chemicals are out (Woodheat poison, EPA best burn).

## Plywood and OSB: not recommended
EPA, NRCan, CMHC and Drolet all say not to burn plywood, and EPA adds any wood with glue on or in it (EPA best burn, NRCan wood heating, CMHC wood heat, Drolet Part 1). EPA's catalytic-stove guide says plywood and particleboard hold chemicals that are hazardous when burned and inhaled (EPA catalytic). NRCan says burning plywood and particleboard releases a toxic cloud of chemicals, and Drolet says burning such fuels can make more CO than hardwood does (NRCan wood heating, Drolet Part 1). OSB is glued wood too, which EPA's 'any wood with glue on or in it' covers. If it truly is that or freezing, the rest is our own judgement, not a tested rule, and it cuts the harm without removing it: only plain, dry offcuts you are sure are unpainted and untreated (plywood from a deck or dock, or marked treated, is treated wood, which Health Canada says never to burn), a few pieces at a time on top of a hot fire of real wood, in a stove on a sound chimney. Never in an open fireplace, which spills smoke into the room more than a stove (NRCan wood heating), and never in a catalytic stove (EPA catalytic). Keep a working CO alarm in the room, crack a window, and treat the ash as doubtful (see below).

## Paper, cardboard and Christmas trees
- Four or five crumpled sheets of newspaper and dry kindling light a fire (NRCan wood heating). Paper, cardboard, sawdust and wax fire starters are fine for starting (Drolet Part 1).
- Armfuls of cardboard or paper are not fuel: people who have a chimney fire often report burning a lot of paper or kindling just before (CSIA white paper), paper in a fireplace can flash-fire (CPSC 611), and cardboard can clog a catalyst and push smoke into the room (EPA catalytic).
- Glossy and coloured paper: EPA lists the coloured inks on magazines, boxes and wrappers (EPA best burn); printing inks often hold heavy metals (EPA trash burning).
- Dry evergreen boughs can explode when burned and start a house fire, and add creosote (Iowa State trees); they flare out of control and throw sparks into the room or up the chimney onto creosote (CPSC 611).

## Driftwood
Burning salt-water driftwood in a stove makes dioxin (Woodheat poison). DuraVent says sea driftwood is highly corrosive to all types of stainless steel (DuraVent DTC), and in a cookstove combustion chamber at about 660 °C, wood soaked in salt water ate about 0.2 mm off several stainless steels in 500 to 1,000 hours of burning (Aprovecho salt); that is hotter than a chimney flue, so read it as a warning, not a rate for your pipe. EPA's list names ocean driftwood. Wood that has lain in a lake or river is still wet: dry it like any green wood (EPA best burn).

## Coal
EPA's rule for catalytic stoves is no coal unless the stove's permanent label lists it, because other fuels can poison the catalyst or damage the stove (EPA catalytic). Drolet's wood stoves say do not burn coal at all (Drolet Part 1). An emergency-heating guide says coal can be burned in a fireplace or stove if a grate holds it with air circulating underneath (MU GH5118); that is general advice, not for any particular stove. A wood stove whose label doesn't list coal is not rated for it: Drolet puts coal on its do-not-burn list with a warning of more CO than hardwood (Drolet Part 1), and EPA says other fuels may damage the stove (EPA catalytic). Check the label; with no label, burn wood.

## Ash from the wrong fuel
The poisons concentrate in the ash: from treated wood (Health Canada 2011) and from garbage, where dioxin stays in the ash (Woodheat poison). Ash from trash burning can harm people if it is buried or spread in a garden (EPA trash burning). Keep ash from anything doubtful in a lidded metal can outside until it is stone cold (ash holds live embers and gives off CO for days: Drolet Part 1), then bag it, keep it away from children and food gardens, and never use it as fertiliser. Breathed smoke or ash from wood you think was treated: Health Canada says contact a poison centre or doctor (Health Canada 2011).
